The [[FIFA Club World Cup]] is an international [[association football]] competition organised by the Fédération Internationale de Football Association ([[FIFA]]), the sport's global governing body.<ref name="Format">{{cite web |url=https://www.fifa.com/mm/document/tournament/competition/01/95/45/34/regulationsfcwc2012_e.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130328220018/http://www.fifa.com/mm/document/tournament/competition/01/95/45/34/regulationsfcwc2012%5fe.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 28, 2013 |title=FIFA Club World Cup Japan 2012 – Regulations |work=[[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] |format=PDF |accessdate=11 March 2013 }}</ref> The championship was first contested as the FIFA Club World Championship in 2000.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament=107/edition=3692/news/newsid=71334.html |title=Brazil 2000 Final Draw |work=[[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] |date=14 October 1999 |accessdate=6 March 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109024044/http://www.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament%3D107/edition%3D3692/news/newsid%3D71334.html |archivedate=9 November 2013 }}</ref> It was not held between [[2001 FIFA Club World Championship|2001]] and 2004 due to a combination of factors, most importantly the collapse of FIFA's marketing partner [[International Sport and Leisure]].<ref name="FIFA 2001">{{cite web|url=http://de.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament=107/edition=4735/releases/newsid=91574.html |title=FIFA decides to postpone 2001 Club World Championship to 2003 |work=[[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] |date=18 May 2001 |accessdate=6 March 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109023834/http://de.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament%3D107/edition%3D4735/releases/newsid%3D91574.html |archivedate=9 November 2013 }}</ref> Following a change in format which saw the FIFA Club World Championship absorb the [[Intercontinental Cup (1960–2004)|Intercontinental Cup]], it was relaunched in 2005 and took its current name the season afterwards.<ref name="Relaunch">{{cite web|url=https://www.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament=107/edition=4735/releases/newsid=96696.html |title=Toyota confirmed as FIFA Club World Championship 2005 naming partner |work=[[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] |date=15 March 2005 |accessdate=6 March 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109024139/http://www.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament%3D107/edition%3D4735/releases/newsid%3D96696.html |archivedate=9 November 2013 }}</ref>

The current format of the tournament, in use since the competition was revamped ahead of the [[2025 FIFA Club World Cup|2025 edition]], features 32 teams competing for the title at venues within the host nation; 12 teams from [[UEFA|Europe]], 6 from [[CONMEBOL|South America]], 4 from [[Asian Football Confederation|Asia]], 4 from [[Confederation of African Football|Africa]], 4 from [[CONCACAF|North, Central America and Caribbean]], 1 from [[Oceania Football Confederation|Oceania]], and 1 team from the host nation. The teams are drawn into eight groups of four, with each team playing three group stage matches in a [[Round-robin tournament|round-robin]] format. The top two teams from each group advance to the knockout stage, starting with the round of 16 and culminating with the final.<ref name="Format" />

[[Pep Guardiola]] was the first manager to win the tournament on four occasions; he led Spanish club [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] to success in [[2009 FIFA Club World Cup|2009]] and [[2011 FIFA Club World Cup|2011]], coached German side [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] to victory in [[2013 FIFA Club World Cup|2013]], and won a fourth title with English club [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]] to victory in [[2023 FIFA Club World Cup|2023]]. He is also the first manager to win the tournament with three clubs. [[Carlo Ancelotti]] has won three titles (once with [[AC Milan|Milan]] in [[2007 FIFA Club World Cup|2007]], twice with [[Real Madrid CF|Real Madrid]] in [[2014 FIFA Club World Cup|2014]] and [[2022 FIFA Club World Cup|2022]]), [[Zinedine Zidane]] has won two titles (in [[2016 FIFA Club World Cup|2016]] and [[2017 FIFA Club World Cup|2017]], both with Real Madrid), and eleven other managers have each won the competition once. [[Enzo Maresca]] is the most recent manager to have won the FIFA Club World Cup, doing so with [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] in the 2025 edition.

==List of managers in the final==
Brazilian, Spanish and German managers hold the joint-record for most consecutive appearances of winning coaches, with three back-to-back triumphs each; a Brazilian manager won the final in [[2000 FIFA Club World Championship final|2000]], [[2005 FIFA Club World Championship final|2005]] and [[2006 FIFA Club World Cup final|2006]], a Spanish manager did so in [[2009 FIFA Club World Cup final|2009]], [[2010 FIFA Club World Cup final|2010]] and [[2011 FIFA Club World Cup final|2011]], while a German manager accomplished the feat in [[2019 FIFA Club World Cup final|2019]], [[2020 FIFA Club World Cup final|2020]] and [[2021 FIFA Club World Cup final|2021]]. Spanish managers have won also won the most total finals, with six (the aforementioned three, plus in [[2013 FIFA Club World Cup final|2013]], [[2015 FIFA Club World Cup final|2015]] and [[2023 FIFA Club World Cup final|2023]]).

[[Rafael Benítez]] of Spain became the first manager to reach the FIFA Club World Cup final with a foreign club, when English side [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] side lost the 2005 final under his leadership;<ref name="FIFA 2005" /> he led other foreign clubs to the final on two further occasions, winning in 2010 with Italian side [[Inter Milan|Internazionale]] and losing in [[2012 FIFA Club World Cup final|2012]] with English team [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]. [[Alex Ferguson|Sir Alex Ferguson]], [[Pep Guardiola]], [[Carlo Ancelotti]], [[Zinedine Zidane]], [[Santiago Solari]], [[Jürgen Klopp]] and [[Thomas Tuchel]] are the other managers to win the final with a foreign club, with Ancelotti ([[2014 FIFA Club World Cup final|2014]] and [[2022 FIFA Club World Cup final|2022]]), Zidane ([[2016 FIFA Club World Cup final|2016]] and [[2017 FIFA Club World Cup final|2017]]) and Guardiola (2013 and 2023) the only ones to accomplish this on multiple occasions, Ancelotti and  Zidane while managing [[Real Madrid CF|Real Madrid]], and Guardiola while managing [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] and [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]].<ref name="FIFA 2006" /><ref name="FIFA 2008" /><ref name="FIFA 2010" />

Along with Ancelotti and Zidane, Guardiola is the only other manager to have led the same club to the final on more than one occasion, coming out victorious with [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] in 2009 and 2011. He also won the final in 2013 as coach of Bayern Munich and in 2023 as coach of Manchester City, becoming the first manager to win the trophy four times and also the first manager to win the trophy with three clubs.<ref name="FIFA 2009" /><ref name="FIFA 2011" /> 

The inaugural final in 2000 remains the only one to see two managers from the same nation, with both hailing from Brazil.<ref name="FIFA 2000" />

==Results by manager==
[[Pep Guardiola]] is the only manager to have won four FIFA Club World Cups; he won twice with [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]], once with [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] and once with [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]].<ref name="FIFA 2009" /><ref name="FIFA 2011" /> He is also the first manager to win the tournament with three clubs. Guardiola also holds the record for the most appearances in the final, with the aforementioned four. [[Lamine N'Diaye]] of Senegal in [[2010 FIFA Club World Cup final|2010]], [[Faouzi Benzarti]] of Tunisia in [[2013 FIFA Club World Cup final|2013]] and [[Masatada Ishii]] of Japan in [[2016 FIFA Club World Cup final|2016]] were the only non-European and non-South American managers to have appeared in the final. The aforementioned three managers, as well as [[Zoran Mamić]] in [[2018 FIFA Club World Cup final|2018]], [[Ricardo Ferretti]] in [[2020 FIFA Club World Cup final|2020]] and [[Ramón Díaz]] in [[2022 FIFA Club World Cup final|2022]], are the only ones to have led a club outside Europe and South America into the decisive match.<ref name="FIFA 2010" />

==Results by nationality==
Spanish managers have had the most success in the competition, amassing six titles in nine total final appearances. Brazilian and Italian managers have each won four titles, German managers have won three, French managers have won two, and a Scottish manager has won the title once. Argentine managers hold the dubious record of the most losses in the final with six, including defeats in three consecutive editions; a manager from Argentina has only won the competition on one occasion.<ref name="FIFA 2008" /><ref name="FIFA 2009" /><ref name="FIFA 2007" />

==Results by continent==
European managers remain the most successful of the competition, with a total of sixteen titles.<ref name="FIFA 2010" /><ref name="FIFA 2008" /><ref name="FIFA 2009" /><ref name="FIFA 2011" /><ref name="FIFA 2007" /> Their South American counterparts are second with five titles, while Africa has had two managers lead a club into the final, and Asia has had one.<ref name="FIFA 2005" /><ref name="FIFA 2006" /><ref name="FIFA 2010" /><ref name="FIFA 2000" />
